newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission statement on economic forecasts.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission statement on economic forecasts.

text.p: The following is a statement from the European Commission that accompanied the release of its autumn economic forecasts:

"The Commission today published its autumn economic forecasts. The overall picture is positive: economic convergence and progress towards the euro are contributing to stronger growth and the first signs of improvements in employment. For the Union as a whole the autumn forecasts are little changed from the Commission's forecasts published in Spring 1996. Growth is expected to be 1.6% in 1996, 2.3% in 1997 and 2.8% in 1998. Over the three years 1996-98 inclusive, the forecasts indicate a net increase of 2.3 million jobs, which should bring the rate of unemployment down to 10.4% in 1998. Most member states are in the process of making impressive efforts to realise economic convergence, in particular by cutting excessive government deficits. The forecasts for inflation, interest rates and the public finances of Member States confirm the Commission's view that there should be a significant, and probably increasing, number of member states capable of meeting the necessary conditions to participate in the euro from 1 January 1999.

The forecasts were presented by Yves-Thibault de SILGUY, Commissioner for Economic, Monetary and Financial Affairs. The Commission's figures for the first time take account of the budget measures of most member states for 1997. As such they provide an better assessment of countries' economic performance next year, which will be the basis for the decisions by Europe's heads of state and government on the initial group of participating countries in stage 3 of monetary union. However, it is important not to exaggerate the significance of the forecasts since these decisions will be taken at the start of 1998 on the basis of actual outturn figures for 1997.
In line with past practice, the Commission's forecasts also include figures for 1998 prepared on the basis of a scenario of unchanged economic policies.
A picture of improving economic growth

The European economy is emerging from the period of weak growth that started in mid-1995. For the Union as a whole, GDP is expected to rise by 1.6% in 1996, 2.3% in 1997 and 2.8% in 1998. The picture is particularly encouraging in a number of countries for which growth has been revised upwards by comparison with the Commission's Spring forecasts (Germany, Denmark, Ireland, the Netherlands and Sweden). These effects have been offset by downward revisions in the forecasts for Italy. As a result the overall figures for the Union remain broadly in line with the Commission's Spring forecasts.
This positive growth outlook is underpinned by a number of factors:
* strong external demand;
* high profitability of investments;
* historically low rates of inflation;
* falling interest rates (both long and short-term rates) resulting from an improved balance (policy mix) between monetary and budgetary policies and moderate wage developments;
* stable exchange rates which have broadly returned to their levels before the fluctuations of Spring 1995.
Modest increase in employment

A gradual improvement in employment is consistent with the growth forecasts: for the Union as a whole, the Commission expects an increase in employment of 1.6% in 1996-98 or the equivalent of 2.3 million new jobs.

At the level of individual member states, improved job creation in some countries (Ireland, Finland and the UK) is expected to result from strong economic growth, while in others (Spain, the Netherlands) the predominant factor is likely to be labour market reforms. Denmark is also likely to see reduced unemployment, mainly as a result of reduced supply of labour in 1996.

The precondition for sustained reductions in unemployment is a solid economic framework based on low inflation, stable monetary conditions and sound public finances. This is what the convergence criteria for monetary union are designed to achieve, which is why the introduction of the euro is good for jobs. However, member states also need to continue with the process of structural reform, in particular to tackle rigidities in the labour market.
Encouraging progress with convergence

The Commission's forecasts confirm that a significant number of member states should be able to achieve the high degree of sustainable convergence which is needed to participate in EMU from 1 January 1999.

* by 1997, 14 member states are expected to be in a position to meet the criteria for inflation and long-term interest rates (Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Spain, France, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Finland, Sweden and the UK);

* there are today 11 countries whose currencies participate in the Exchange Rate Mechanism of the EMS (Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Spain, France, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal and Finland);

* 12 countries are expected to have an annual public deficit of 3% of GDP or less in 1997 (Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Spain, France, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Finland and Sweden).

The average deficit/GDP ratio for the Union as a whole is expected to reach 3% in 1997 (down from 5% in 1995) and to fall further to 2.5% of GDP in 1998 underlining a continuing trend of improvements in member states' budgetary positions;

* while the outstanding stock of debt in most countries is expected to remain above the reference value of 60% of GDP, in many cases it is likely to be on a downward trend (and in some countries could be lower still when intended privatisation plans are realised).

In line with past practice, the Commission's forecasts take account of measures which have already been implemented or have been presented in detail and are backed with a sufficient degree of political commitment.

This is particularly relevant in relation to Member states' budgetary proposals for 1997, many of which are in the course of adoption by national parliaments. The Commission's forecasts also take account of decisions taken by Eurostat on the compatibility of treasury transactions with the rules for the public deficit contained in the Treaty and the European System of Integrated Economic Accounts. Two specific cases are highlighted:

* the planned payment in 1997 from France Telecom to the national budget of FF37.5 billion to cover future pension liabilities for France Telecom employees. This measure is fully reflected in the Commission's figures for the French deficit in 1997 following a recent decision by Eurostat. This is clearly a one-off transaction which affects only the figures for 1997;

* measures planned by the Italian authorities to meet the objectives fixed by the 1997 budget law. The Commission's forecasts reflect those measures which appear consistent with the relevant accounting definitions (amounting to 0.3% of GDP) but not those which are still subject to a technical examination by Eurostat.

The Treaty requires countries to demonstrate a high degree of sustainable convergence in order to participate in EMU. This means that any one-off measures should be complemented with other measures in order to achieve budgetary rigour thereafter. In this context, the scenario for 1998 indicating further improvements in member states' budgetary situations is encouraging. The Commission's proposals for a stability pact to ensure lasting budgetary discipline in stage 3 of monetary union are also designed with this aim in mind."
